items.entry: Impliquer les joueurs. Réfléchissez à la façon dont les personnages seront entraînés dans la situation que vous avez établie. Considérez comment l'aventure pourrait se lier aux objectifs des personnages.

items.name: Étape 3 :
items.entry: Planifier les rencontres. Déterminez les rencontres ou événements qui mènent les personnages du début de l'aventure à sa fin.

items.name: Étape 4 :
items.entry: Conclure. Comment vous attendez-vous à ce que l'aventure se termine ? Réfléchissez aux fins possibles ainsi qu'aux récompenses pour les personnages.

entries: The rest of this chapter offers inspiration and advice for each of these four steps.

entries.name: Utiliser des aventures publiées
entries: A published adventure includes a pregenerated scenario with the maps, NPCs, monsters, and treasures you need to run it. This allows you to focus your preparation time on plot developments that arise from the characters' actions.

You can adjust a published adventure so it better suits your campaign and appeals to your players. For example, you can replace the villain of an adventure with one the players have already encountered in your campaign, or add details from your campaign setting so the adventure involves your players' characters in ways that the adventure's designer never could have imagined.

Published adventures also provide inspiration for your own adventures. You can even take a part of an adventure and incorporate it into a different one. For example, you might use a map of a temple but repopulate it with monsters of your choice, or you might use a chase sequence as a model for a pursuit scene in your campaign.

entries.name: Établir le postulat
entries: An adventure shares many of the features of a novel, a movie, an issue of a comic, or an episode of a TV show. Comic series and serialized TV dramas are particularly good comparisons because of the way individual adventures are limited in scope but blend together (to some degree) to create a larger narrative. If an adventure is a single episode or season of a series, a campaign is the series as a whole.

But while it's worthwhile to compare an adventure to these other forms of storytelling, remember that an adventure isn't a complete story until you play it. Your players are coauthors of the story with you, and the events of the story shouldn't be predetermined; the actions of the players' characters have to matter. For example, if a major villain shows up before the end of the adventure, the adventure should allow for the possibility that the heroes defeat that villain. Otherwise, players can feel as if they've been railroaded—set onto a course that has only one destination or outcome, no matter how hard they try to change it.

You might find it helpful to think about an adventure not as a narrative that arcs from beginning to end with little chance for deviation, but more in terms of situations that you are presenting to the characters. The adventure unfolds organically from the players' responses to the situations you present.

entries.name: Gardefous et rails
entries: Players need to feel like they're in control of their characters, the choices they make matter, and what they do has some effect on the outcome of the adventure and on the game world. Keep that in mind as you're planning adventures. If your adventure relies on certain events, plan for multiple ways they might come about, or be prepared for clever players to prevent those events from happening as you expect. Otherwise, your players might end up feeling railroaded.

On the flip side, players sometimes willfully disregard the adventure hooks you put in front of them and go entirely off the rails. See "{@book Respect for the DM|XDMG|0|Respect for the DM}" in {@book chapter 1|XDMG|0} and "{@book Draw In the Players|XDMG|3|Draw In the Players}" later in this chapter for advice about dealing with this situation.

One way to give players impactful choices is to keep multiple adventure possibilities available to them at the same time. If the characters have two or three things they can investigate or pursue, they have a meaningful choice. And if whatever threads they don't investigate turn into bigger problems, you've clearly demonstrated that their decisions matter.

entries.name: Postulat de l'aventure
entries: One way to start brainstorming an adventure is to imagine a situation that might pique the characters' interest. For some D&D players, a rumor of a dungeon filled with treasure is enough of a premise to launch an adventure. A brewing war between two small nations, the death of a leader and the accession of a new one, a migration of dangerous monsters, the appearance of a comet, and the opening of a portal to another plane of existence are other situations that could lead to adventure.

A simple premise might also boil down to "a magic item that the characters want is hidden away in a dungeon." Browsing the magic items in {@book chapter 7|XDMG|6} can inspire you to create a simple adventure seed.

entries.name: Conflit de l'aventure
entries: A premise can be a good starting point, but before you can turn it into an adventure, it needs a conflict worthy of the heroes' attention. The conflict might be driven by a single villain or monster, a villain with lackeys, an assortment of monsters, or an evil organization. But it need not involve the forces of evil; it could be a rivalry or disagreement between two families, organizations, or nations; a looming natural (or magical) disaster; or even conflict within the adventuring party about how to pursue the characters' goals.

Given a premise of a dungeon filled with treasure, what conflict awaits the characters when they enter the dungeon? That might be as simple as "hostile monsters want to eat the characters" or "two rival factions of monsters inhabit the dungeon." It might also involve a rival or a villain hoping to plunder the dungeon first, a rumbling volcano threatening to erupt and bury the dungeon, or two rival families claiming ownership of the treasure left behind in the dungeon by their ancestors.
If you're stuck, browse through the {@book Monster Manual|XMM} until you find a monster that inspires you.

entries.name: Situations d'aventure par niveau
entries: Use the tables in this section to inspire adventure ideas for characters of different levels, with the range of possible levels grouped into four tiers. You can roll on the tables and see if the result sparks your imagination or read the entries on the tables until you find something that grabs you.

entries.name: Niveaux 1–4 : Héros locaux
entries: The fate of a village might depend on the abilities of fledgling adventurers. These characters navigate dangerous terrain and explore haunted crypts, where they might fight ferocious wolves, giant spiders, evil cultists, flesh-eating ghouls, and ruthless brigands.

entries.caption: Situations d'aventure (niveaux 1–4)
rows: A dragon wyrmling has gathered a band of kobolds to help it amass a hoard.
Wererats living in a city's sewers plot to take control of the governing council.
Bandit activity signals efforts to revive an evil cult long ago driven from the region.
A pack of gnolls is rampaging dangerously close to local farmlands.
A rivalry between two merchant families escalates from mischief to mayhem.
A new sinkhole has revealed a long-buried dungeon thought to hold treasure.
Miners discovered an underground ruin and were captured by monsters living there.
An innocent person is being framed for the crimes of a shape-shifting monster.
Ghouls are venturing out of the catacombs at night.
A notorious criminal hides from the law in an old ruin or abandoned mine.
A contagion in a forest is causing spiders to grow massive and become aggressive.
To take revenge against a village for an imagined slight, a necromancer has been animating the corpses in the village cemetery.
An evil cult is spreading in a village. Those who oppose the cult are marked for sacrifice.
An abandoned house on the edge of town is haunted by Undead because of a cursed item in the house.
Creatures from the Feywild enter the world and cause mischief and misfortune among villagers and their livestock.
A hag's curse is making animals unusually aggressive.
Bullies have appointed themselves the village militia and are extorting money and food from villagers.
After a local fisher pulls a grotesque statue from the sea, aquatic monsters start attacking the waterfront at night.
The ruins on the hill near the village lie under a curse, so people don't go there—except a scholar who wants to study the ruins.
A new captain has taken charge of a band of pirates or bandits and started raiding more frequently.

entries.name: Niveaux 5–10 : Héros du royaume
entries: At this tier, characters undertake adventures that might determine the fate of a region. These adventurers venture into fearsome wilds and ancient ruins, where they confront giants, hydras, golems, devils, demons, and mind flayers. They might also face a young dragon that has just established a lair.

entries.caption: Situations d'aventure (niveaux 5–10)
rows: A group of cultists has summoned a demon to wreak havoc in the city.
A rebel lures monsters to the cause with the promise of looting the king's treasury.
An evil Artifact has transformed a forest into a dismal swamp full of horrific monsters.
An Aberration living in the Underdark sends minions to capture people from the surface to turn those people into new minions.
A monster (perhaps a devil, slaad, or hag) is impersonating a prominent noble to throw the realm into civil war.
A master thief plans to steal royal regalia.
A golem intended to serve as a protector has gone berserk and captured its creator.
A conspiracy of spies, assassins, and necromancers schemes to overthrow a ruler.
After establishing a lair, a young dragon is trying to earn the fear and respect of other creatures living nearby.
The approach of a lone giant alarms the people of a town, but the giant is simply looking for a place to live in peace.
An enormous monster on display in a menagerie breaks free and goes on a rampage.
A coven of hags steals cherished memories from travelers.
A villain seeks powerful magic in an ancient ruin, hoping to use it to conquer the region.
A scheming aristocrat hosts a masquerade ball, which many guests see as an opportunity to advance their own agendas. At least one shape-shifting monster also attends.
A ship carrying a valuable treasure or an evil Artifact sinks in a storm or monster attack.
A natural disaster was actually caused by magic gone awry or a cult's villainous plans.
A secretive cult uses spies to heighten tensions between two rival nations, hoping to provoke a war that will weaken both.
Rebels or forces of an enemy nation have kidnapped an important noble.
The descendants of a displaced people want to reclaim their ancestral city, which is now inhabited by monsters.
A renowned group of adventurers never returned from an expedition to a famous ruin.

entries.name: Niveaux 11–16 : Maîtres du royaume

entries.title: La mort d'un dragon ancien peut ébranler les fondations du monde

entries: The fate of a nation or even the world depends on the characters at this tier. These adventurers explore uncharted regions and delve into forgotten dungeons, where the characters confront terrible schemers of the Lower Planes, cunning rakshasas and beholders, and hungry purple worms. They might encounter and even defeat a powerful adult dragon. At this tier, they broker peace between nations or lead them into war, and their formidable reputations attract the attention of powerful foes.

entries.caption: Situations d'aventure (niveaux 11–16)
rows: A portal to the Abyss opens in a cursed location and spews demons into the world.
A band of hunting giants has driven its prey—enormous beasts—into pastureland.
An adult dragon's lair is transforming an expanse into an environment inhospitable to the other creatures living there.
A long-lost journal describes an incredible journey to a hidden subterranean realm full of magical wonders.
Cultists hope to persuade a dragon to undergo the rite that will transform it into a dracolich.
The ruler of the realm is sending an emissary to a hostile neighbor to negotiate a truce, and the emissary needs protection.
A castle or city has been drawn into another plane of existence.
A storm tears across the land, with a mysterious flying citadel in the eye of the storm.
Two parts of a magic item are in the hands of bitter enemies; the third piece is lost.
Evil cultists gather from around the world to summon a monstrous god or alien entity.
A tyrannical ruler outlaws the use of magic without official sanction. A secret society of spellcasters seeks to oust the tyrant.
During a drought, low water levels in a lake reveal previously unknown ancient ruins that contain a powerful evil.

entries.name: Niveaux 17–20 : Maîtres du monde
entries: At this tier, adventures have far-reaching consequences, possibly determining the fate of millions on the Material Plane and even places beyond. Characters traverse otherworldly realms and explore demiplanes and other extraplanar locales, where they fight terrible balor demons, titans, archdevils, liches, ancient dragons, and even manifestations of the gods.

entries.caption: Situations d'aventure (niveaux 17–20)
rows: An ancient dragon is scheming to destroy a god and take the god's place in the pantheon. The dragon's minions are searching for Artifacts that can summon and weaken this god.
A band of giants drove away a metallic dragon and took over the dragon's lair, and the dragon wants to reclaim the lair.
An ancient hero returns from the dead to prepare the world for the return of an equally ancient monster.
An ancient Artifact has the power to defeat or imprison a rampaging titan.
A god of agriculture is angry, causing rivers to dry up and crops to wither.
An Artifact belonging to a god falls into mortal hands.
A titan imprisoned in the Underdark begins to break free, causing terrible earthquakes that are only a hint of the destruction that the titan will cause if it is released.
A lich tries to exterminate any spellcasters that approach the lich's level of power.
A holy temple was built around a portal leading to one of the Lower Planes to prevent any evil from passing through in either direction. Now the temple has come under siege from both directions.
Five ancient metallic dragons lair in the Pillars of Creation. If all these dragons are killed, the world will collapse into chaos. One has just been slain.

entries.name: Cadre de l'aventure
entries: Many D&D adventures revolve around dungeons—interior spaces such as great halls and tombs, subterranean monster lairs, mazes riddled with traps, natural caverns extending for miles beneath the surface, and ruined castles. The "{@book Dungeons|XDMG|2|Dungeons}" section in {@book chapter 3|XDMG|2} can help you craft a dungeon environment for an adventure.

Of course, not every adventure takes place in a dungeon. A wilderness trek across the desert or a harrowing journey into the jungle can be an exciting adventure in its own right. Outdoors, dragons wheel across the sky in search of prey, fierce warriors pour forth from grim fortresses to wage war against their neighbors, ogres and trolls plunder farmsteads for food, and monstrous spiders drop from web-shrouded trees.

Adventures can also take place in cities, towns, and villages, which are often no less dangerous than dungeons or the wilds. The "{@book Settlements|XDMG|2|Settlements}" section in {@book chapter 3|XDMG|2} can help you create a settlement where an adventure can take place.

entries.name: Écrire pour soi
entries: When you're preparing an adventure to run for your friends, you don't need to write hundreds of pages describing each location in exhaustive detail. You can run a game with no more written notes than you'll find in one of the short adventures at the end of this chapter.

entries.name: Cartes d'aventure
entries: An adventure location almost always benefits from a map, and the more thoughtfully constructed the map is, the more fun players are likely to have as their characters explore the location.

entries.name: Cartes et structure de l'aventure
entries: An adventure map can take many forms—from a detailed dungeon map that shows the dimensions and contents of every room to a rough outline of how one encounter might lead to another, depending on the route the characters choose. Whatever form your map takes, it functions as a flowchart since each decision point (a branch in a corridor, a room with multiple exits) leads to new decision points. If the characters leave a room by the north door, you check your map and determine it leads them into the great hall, lined with pillars, where the fire giant king holds court. If they leave by the secret door to the southeast, you check the map and follow the secret tunnel as it winds to the hidden vaults below the great hall.

entries.name: Cartes d'exemple
entries: {@book Appendix B|XDMG|9} contains maps you can use for your adventures or as inspiration for your own maps. You can also modify those maps to fit the details of the location you have in mind.

entries.name: Inspiration cartographique
entries: The internet is a great place to find adventure maps that have been made available, as well as real-world building floor plans and city maps and other images that can inspire your mapmaking.

entries.name: Donner vie à un lieu
entries: An inhabited adventure location has its own ecosystem. The creatures that live there need to eat, drink, breathe, and sleep. Predators need prey, and intelligent creatures search for lairs offering the best combination of air, food, water, and security. Keep these factors in mind when designing an adventure location. If the site has an internal logic, adventurers can use their understanding of that logic to make informed decisions.

For example, characters who find a pool of fresh water in a dungeon might infer that many of the creatures inhabiting the dungeon come to that spot to drink. The adventurers might set an ambush at the pool. Likewise, closed or locked doors can restrict the movement of some creatures. A dungeon infested with carrion crawlers or stirges would need open passages so that these creatures can move about to find food.

entries.title: Symboles cartographiques courants

entries.name: Habitants de l'aventure
entries: The monsters in any adventure location are more than a collection of random creatures that happen to live near one another. Fungi, natural animals, scavengers, and predators can coexist in a complex ecology, alongside sapient creatures who share living space through some combination of negotiation and domination.

Each creature's entry in the {@book Monster Manual|XMM} indicates the terrain types where that creature is most often found, and that book also includes tables listing the creatures commonly found within each type of terrain. Using that information, you can decide which creatures inhabit an adventure location within a particular environment. You can choose a range of creatures, from common vermin to sapient inhabitants and terrifying predators, and decide how they live together.

entries.name: Factions
entries: Particularly in larger areas, groups of creatures might compete for resources. When these groups consist of sapient creatures, opportunities abound for the adventurers who enter those areas. Characters might ally with one group or play groups against each other to reduce the threat of the more powerful monsters. For example, in a dungeon inhabited by mind flayers and the grimlocks they rule, the adventurers might try to incite the grimlocks to revolt against the mind flayers.

Bring the NPC leaders of groups to life as described in the "{@book Nonplayer Characters|XDMG|2|Nonplayer Characters}" section in {@book chapter 3|XDMG|2}, fleshing out their personalities and goals. Then use those elements to decide how those leaders respond to adventurers.

entries.name: Impliquer les joueurs
entries: If an adventure situation directly affects the characters or the people and places they care about, that is often enough motivation for the characters to get involved. (However, see "{@book Respect for the Players|XDMG|0|Respect for the Players}" in {@book chapter 1|XDMG|0} for advice about harming the people and places characters love.)

If the adventure situation doesn't have an obvious impact on the characters or the people or things they care about, you can use other techniques to draw in the players. These are best tailored to the motivations of your players and their characters. For example, some adventuring groups are noble heroes who respond without hesitation to the pleas of innocent villagers crying for help; other groups are hardened mercenaries who respond only to offers of payment. Some groups are devoted to gods, rulers, or other patrons who might send them on quests, either directly or through intermediaries.

entries.name: Détourner les clichés
entries: As you populate your world with interesting supporting characters, consider the following:

items.name: Éviter les stéréotypes
items.entry: Montrez comment plusieurs personnes d'une même culture diffèrent. N'utilisez pas un accent réel de façon dénigrante.

items.name: Une belle diversité
items.entry: Mettez en scène des personnes de genres, d'ethnies et de sexualités différentes, ainsi que des personnes aux croyances, capacités, rôles, professions, intérêts et visions variés.

items.name: Regard neuf
items.entry: Chaque fois que possible, apportez un regard neuf à un trope familier. La figure mystérieuse qui confie une quête aux aventuriers au nom du roi pourrait être le roi déguisé. Le magicien de la tour pourrait être une illusion projetée créée par une bande de voleurs pour garder leur butin.

items.name: Empathie
items.entry: Traitez les PNJ comme de vraies personnes avec de vraies motivations. Mettez-vous à leur place. Que feriez-vous ?

entries.name: Patrons de l'aventure
entries: Many adventures begin with a patron asking the characters to undertake a quest or mission, offering a reward in exchange for this service.

Take the time to flesh out an NPC who serves as a patron. Once in a while, it can be interesting for the characters' patron to betray them. Pulling that trick more than once in a campaign, though, is likely to make the players unwilling to trust any future patrons and possibly suspicious about any adventure hooks you put in front of them.

The Patron Hooks table offers some suggestions for ways a patron can lead characters to an adventure situation. The "{@book Campaign Start|XDMG|4|Campaign Start}" section in {@book chapter 5|XDMG|4} offers some more suggestions for patrons.

entries.caption: Amorces de patrons
rows: A town crier announces that someone is hoping to hire adventurers.
Someone the characters want to impress or need a favor from asks them to deal with the adventure situation.
When the characters arrive in a new city, they find a job board where someone has posted in search of adventurers.
A wealthy patron who is aware of the adventurers' accomplishments writes to them, offering to pay them for their talents.
A citizen in need, who has learned of the adventurers' accomplishments and kindness, travels miles to find them and implore them for help.
The adventurers are arrested (on valid or invented charges) and offered a chance to escape punishment by completing a quest.

entries.title: Lorsque des factions rivales habitent un donjon en ruine, parfois le mieux est de rester à l’écart !

entries.name: Amorces surnaturelles
entries: Celestial omens, vivid dreams, or other magical phenomena can point characters to the adventure situation and suggest a course of action. The Supernatural Hooks table offers some suggestions.

entries.caption: Amorces surnaturelles
rows: The characters all have a vivid dream that foreshadows elements of the adventure.
While preparing spells, one character receives a quest from a god or patron.
A fortune teller's reading for one of the characters points to a quest and offers hints about challenges that lie ahead.
Flames, clouds, smoke, or huge flocks of birds take distinct shapes that portend the adventure situation.
Animals or animated objects speak clearly to direct the adventurers toward the situation.
Someone who died returns as a ghost and haunts the characters. The ghost prompts the characters to investigate the cause of the ghost's death and put it to rest.

entries.name: Amorces fortuites
entries: Sometimes, characters just happen on an adventure through sheer coincidence—or at least what appears to be coincidence (which might actually involve divine or other supernatural intervention). The Happenstance Hooks table provides some ideas.

entries.caption: Amorces fortuites
rows: The characters find a letter describing the adventure situation.
The characters are on an unrelated quest, such as searching for a particular magic item, that leads them into the adventure situation.
The adventure situation disrupts a festival or ceremony that the characters are attending.
A magical mishap places the characters in the adventure situation.
While traveling in a caravan or aboard a ship, the characters befriend an NPC who has news about the adventure situation.
The characters are attacked after being mistaken for another group of adventurers. They learn about the adventure situation from a clue left behind by their attackers.

entries.name: Planifier les rencontres
entries: Encounters are the individual scenes in the larger story of your adventure. Reduced to fundamentals, an encounter is an objective with an obstacle. It accomplishes one or more of the following:

items: Moving characters closer to achieving a goal
Frustrating the characters' progress toward a goal

entries.name: Objectifs des personnages
entries: The following objectives can be foundations for encounters. Although these objectives focus on a single encounter during an adventure, using the same objective in multiple encounters allows you to combine these encounters into a larger obstacle or problem the adventurers must overcome.

entries.name: Conclure la paix
entries: The characters must convince two opposing groups (or their leaders) to end the conflict that embroils them. As a complication, the characters might have enemies on one or both of the opposing sides, or some other group or individual might be instigating the conflict to further its own ends. An encounter aimed at making peace might involve only social interaction, perhaps with the threat of combat if negotiations go poorly. It could also begin as a combat encounter, with the characters trying to stop the fighting and get the parties talking to each other.

entries.name: Protéger un PNJ ou un objet
entries: The characters must act as bodyguards or protect some object in their custody. As a complication, an NPC under the party's protection might be cursed, panicked, unable to fight, or apt to risk the lives of the adventurers through dubious decisions. The object the adventurers have sworn to protect might be sentient, cursed, or difficult to transport. Such an encounter might be a combat encounter or an exploration encounter, with either {@variantrule Hostile [Attitude]|XPHB|Hostile} monsters or a dangerous environment threatening the NPC or object the characters are trying to protect. If the characters are protecting an NPC, this objective can add an element of social interaction to a combat or exploration encounter.

entries.name: Récupérer un objet
entries: The adventurers must gain possession of a specific object in the area of the encounter, often with a time limit. This might be a combat encounter, with monsters protecting the object, or an exploration encounter, with traps or hazards preventing access to the object. As a complication, enemies might desire the object as much as the adventurers do, adding a combat element to an exploration encounter or complicating a combat.

entries.name: Traverser un parcours d'obstacles
entries: The adventurers must pass through a dangerous area. As with retrieving an object, reaching the exit is a higher priority than killing opponents in the area. A time limit adds a complication, as does a decision point that might lead characters astray. This might be an exploration encounter, with traps and hazards as complications, or a combat encounter against {@variantrule Hostile [Attitude]|XPHB|Hostile} monsters.

entries.name: S'infiltrer
entries: The adventurers need to move through the encounter area without their enemies noticing. This is typically an exploration encounter, but if the characters are detected, a combat encounter or social interaction might result.

entries.name: Interrompre un rituel
entries: The plots of evil cult leaders, malevolent spellcasters, and Fiends often involve rituals that must be foiled. In a combat encounter, characters might have to fight their way through evil minions before attempting to disrupt the ritual's magic. This could also drive an exploration encounter, where the challenge is getting to the place where the ritual is occurring, or a social interaction encounter, where the objective is convincing the ritual leaders to stop their rite. As a complication, the ritual might be close to completion when the characters arrive, imposing a time limit. The ritual's completion might have immediate consequences, too.

entries.name: Neutraliser une cible unique
entries: A villain the characters seek to defeat is surrounded by minions powerful enough to kill the adventurers. The characters can flee and hope to confront the villain another day, or they can try to fight their way through the minions. As a complication, the minions might be innocent creatures under the villain's control. Killing the villain means breaking that control, but the adventurers must endure the minions' attacks until the villain falls.

entries.title: Des pillards gobilins préparent une embuscade dans un défilé

entries.name: Garder l'aventure en mouvement
entries: Make sure your players have clear objectives they can pursue at every stage of the adventure. Three simple techniques can ensure that the players understand the task at hand and how to pursue it:

items.name: PNJ conseillers
items.entry: Un PNJ serviable lors d'une interaction sociale peut offrir conseils et suggestions aux personnages. Un tel PNJ peut être le patron qui a initialement envoyé les personnages en aventure, quelqu'un qu'ils ont rencontré en chemin, ou un contact d'un personnage. Lorsque vous planifiez une aventure, incluez des PNJ capables de remplir ce rôle.

items.name: Intrusion maléfique
items.entry: Si la partie commence à s'enliser, faites rencontrer aux personnages un sbire ou un monstre lié à la menace principale de l'aventure. À la fin de la rencontre, les personnages trouvent peut-être une information qui les remet sur la bonne voie. Planifiez une ou deux rencontres de ce type à l'avance.

items.name: Le rôle du MJ
items.entry: Si les personnages ne parviennent pas à comprendre comment résoudre une rencontre ou ne savent quoi faire ensuite, vous pouvez rappeler aux joueurs ce que leurs personnages ont déjà appris ou demander des tests d'Intelligence ({@skill Investigation|XPHB}) ou similaires pour voir si leurs personnages peuvent se souvenir et relier des éléments que les joueurs pourraient négliger.

entries.name: De quoi satisfaire tout le monde
entries: As described in the "{@book Know Your Players|XDMG|1|Know Your Players}" section in {@book chapter 2|XDMG|1}, players have different tastes in the activities they enjoy in the game. An adventure needs to account for the different players and characters in your group to draw them into the story.

An adventure that includes a balance of exploration, social interaction, and combat is likely to appeal to a wide breadth of players. But an adventure you create for your home campaign doesn't have to appeal to every possible player interest—only to the players at your table.

You can design encounters that appeal to multiple player motivations. Imagine a fight pitting the characters against a gang of gnolls, delighting the players who enjoy fighting. Then a young dragon wanders into the middle of the fight. Suddenly the fight can swing one of two ways: the dragon could help the gnolls against the party or help the party against the gnolls. It's up to the players who thrive on acting to persuade the dragon to help the party.

entries.name: Plusieurs voies pour progresser
entries: Make sure there are multiple ways the characters can progress through the adventure at any point, so if they miss one way, they have an alternative. Plan opportunities for the adventure to move forward even when the characters fail. Use challenges with a single path to success only as chances for the characters to obtain extra rewards.

entries.name: Rencontres d'interaction sociale
entries: The "{@book Running Social Interaction|XDMG|1|Running Social Interaction}" section in {@book chapter 2|XDMG|1} offers advice for handling social interaction encounters and can help you craft these encounters. The "{@book Nonplayer Characters|XDMG|2|Nonplayer Characters}" section in {@book chapter 3|XDMG|2} is also essential for creating these encounters.

entries.name: Rencontres d'exploration
entries: An encounter centered on exploration might involve the characters trying to disarm a trap, find a secret door, or discover something about the adventure location. An exploration encounter could also involve the characters spending a day crossing a rolling plain or traversing vast caverns.

The "{@book Running Exploration|XDMG|1|Running Exploration}" section in {@book chapter 2|XDMG|1} can help you craft these encounters as well as run them. Various sections in {@book chapter 3|XDMG|2} can also help you detail obstacles and dangers in an exploration encounter: see "{@book Chases|XDMG|2|Chases}," "{@book Curses and Magical Contagions|XDMG|2|Curses and Magical Contagions}," "{@book Doors|XDMG|2|Doors}," "{@book Environmental Effects|XDMG|2|Environmental Effects}," "{@book Hazards|XDMG|2|Hazards}," "{@book Poison|XDMG|2|Poison}," and "{@book Traps|XDMG|2|Traps}" in particular.

entries.name: Rencontres de combat

entries.title: La conversation d'Otto avec un miroir magique est une rencontre d'interaction sociale palpitante

entries: The following features can make a combat encounter more interesting or challenging:

items.name: Variations d'élévation
items.entry: Les éléments de terrain offrant un changement d'élévation (comme des piles de caisses vides, des rebords et des balcons) récompensent le positionnement astucieux et incitent les personnages à sauter, grimper, voler ou se téléporter.

items.name: Positions défensives
items.entry: Les ennemis placés dans des endroits difficiles d'accès ou des positions défensives forcent les personnages qui attaquent normalement à distance à se déplacer.

items.name: Dangers environnementaux
items.entry: La section « {@book Hazards|XDMG|2|Dangers environnementaux} » du {@book chapitre 3|XDMG|2} décrit des éléments dangereux, comme des plaques de gluant vert, dont les personnages ou leurs ennemis peuvent tirer parti.

items.name: Groupes de monstres mixtes
items.entry: Lorsque différents types de monstres coopèrent, ils peuvent combiner leurs capacités — à l'image de personnages aux classes et origines différentes. Une force diverse est plus puissante.

items.name: Raisons de bouger
items.entry: Utilisez des éléments qui incitent les personnages et leurs ennemis à se déplacer, comme des lustres, des tonneaux de poudre ou d'huile, et des pièges à rocher roulant.

entries.name: Difficulté des rencontres de combat
entries: Use the following guidelines to create a combat encounter of a desired level of difficulty.

entries.name: Étape 1 : Choisir une difficulté
entries: Three categories describe the range of encounter difficulty:

items.name: Difficulté faible
items.entry: Une rencontre de difficulté faible comporte probablement un ou deux moments effrayants pour les joueurs, mais leurs personnages devraient en sortir victorieux sans pertes. Un ou plusieurs d'entre eux pourraient toutefois avoir besoin d'utiliser des ressources de soin. En règle approximative, un monstre solitaire constitue généralement un défi de difficulté faible pour un groupe de quatre personnages dont le niveau égale le FP du monstre.

items.name: Difficulté modérée
items.entry: Sans soins ni autres ressources, une rencontre de difficulté modérée pourrait mal tourner pour les aventuriers. Les personnages les plus faibles pourraient être mis hors de combat, et il existe une faible chance qu'un ou plusieurs personnages meurent.

items.name: Difficulté élevée
items.entry: Une rencontre de difficulté élevée pourrait être fatale à un ou plusieurs personnages. Pour y survivre, les personnages auront besoin de tactiques avisées, de réflexes rapides, et peut-être même d'un peu de chance.

entries.name: Étape 2 : Déterminer votre budget de PX
entries: Using the XP Budget per Character table, cross-reference the party's level with the desired encounter difficulty. Multiply the number in the table by the number of characters in the party to get your XP budget for the encounter.

entries.name: Étape 3 : Dépenser votre budget
entries: Every creature has an XP value in its stat block. When you add a creature to your combat encounter, deduct its XP from your XP budget to determine how many XP you have left to spend. Spend as much of your XP budget as you can without going over. It's OK if you have a few unspent XP left over. Examples are given below:

items.name: Exemple 1
items.entry: Une rencontre de difficulté faible pour quatre personnages de niveau 1 dispose d'un budget de PX de 50 × 4, soit 200 PX au total. Avec cela, vous pourriez construire l'une quelconque des rencontres suivantes :

items: 2 {@creature Guêpe géante|XMM|Giant Wasps} (100 XP each), for 200 XP total
6 {@creature Fléau des brindilles|XMM|Twig Blights} (25 XP each), for 150 XP total

items.name: Exemple 2
items.entry: Une rencontre de difficulté modérée pour cinq personnages de niveau 3 dispose d'un budget de PX de 225 × 5, soit 1 125 PX au total. Avec cela, vous pourriez construire l'une ou l'autre de ces rencontres :

items: 2 {@creature Nothic|XMM|Nothics} (450 XP each) and 9 {@creature Stirge|XMM|Stirges} (25 XP each), for 1,125 XP total
1 {@creature Wight|XMM} (700 XP), 1 {@creature Squelette de cheval de guerre|XMM} (100 XP), and 6 {@creature Squelette|XMM|Skeletons} (50 XP each), for 1,100 XP total

items.name: Exemple 3
items.entry: Une rencontre de difficulté élevée pour six personnages de niveau 15 dispose d'un budget de PX de 7 800 × 6, soit 46 800 PX au total. Avec cela, vous pourriez construire cette rencontre :

items: 2 {@creature Dragon rouge adulte|XMM|Adult Red Dragons} (18,000 XP each) and 2 {@creature Géant du feu|XMM|Fire Giants} (5,000 XP each), for 46,000 XP total

entries.name: Résolution de problèmes
entries: When creating and running combat encounters, keep the following in mind.

entries.name: Beaucoup de créatures
entries: The more creatures in an encounter, the higher the risk that a lucky streak on their part could deal more damage to the characters than you expect. If your encounter includes more than two creatures per character, include fragile creatures that can be defeated quickly. This guideline is especially important for characters of level 1 or 2.

entries.name: Ajustements
entries: A player's absence might warrant removing creatures from an encounter to keep it at the intended difficulty. Also, die rolls and other factors can result in an encounter being easier or harder than intended. You can adjust an encounter on the fly, such as by having creatures flee (making the encounter easier) or adding reinforcements (making the encounter harder).

entries.name: Créatures de FP 0
entries: Creatures that have a CR of 0, particularly ones that are worth 0 XP, should be used sparingly. If you want to include many CR 0 critters in an encounter, use swarms from the {@book Monster Manual|XMM} instead.

entries.name: Nombre de blocs de statistiques
entries: The best combat encounters often pair one kind of creature with another, such as fire giants paired with hell hounds. Be mindful of the number of stat blocks you need to run the encounter. Referencing more than two or three stat blocks for a single encounter can be daunting, particularly if the creatures are complex.

entries.name: Créatures puissantes
entries: If your combat encounter includes a creature whose CR is higher than the party's level, be aware that such a creature might deal enough damage with a single action to take out one or more characters. For example, an {@creature Ogre|XMM} (CR 2) can kill a level 1 Wizard with a single blow.

entries.name: Capacités inhabituelles
entries: If a monster has a feature that lower-level characters can't easily overcome, consider not adding that monster to an encounter for characters whose level is lower than the monster's Challenge Rating.

entries.name: Comportement des monstres
entries: The attitudes, motivations, and behavior of the monsters in an encounter help determine how a social interaction plays out (and whether it might erupt into combat) and influence the course of combat.

entries.title: Des kobolds dressent une barricade pour tenir les aventuriers à distance

entries.name: Attitudes initiales
entries: A published adventure typically notes or implies whether a creature's initial attitude toward the adventurers is {@variantrule Friendly [Attitude]|XPHB|Friendly}, {@variantrule Indifferent [Attitude]|XPHB|Indifferent}, or {@variantrule Hostile [Attitude]|XPHB|Hostile}. In an encounter you've created, you can decide that starting attitude, or you can randomly determine it using the Initial Attitude table.

entries.caption: Attitude initiale
footnotes: *Roll different dice to alter the range and likelihood of possible attitudes. For example, you could roll {@dice 1d6} for a predatory monster, {@dice 1d6 + 3} for ordinary travelers, or {@dice 1d6 + 6} for kindhearted individuals.

entries.name: Personnalité des monstres
entries: If an encounter involves a significant individual, use the guidance in the "{@book Nonplayer Characters|XDMG|2|Nonplayer Characters}" section of {@book chapter 3|XDMG|2} to flesh out the details of that individual's personality and aims. For a group of nameless monsters, you can decide on a personality based on the monsters' entries in the {@book Monster Manual|XMM}, or you can use the Monster Personality table to inform how you portray the monsters and their actions. It's simplest to assign the same personality traits to an entire group of monsters in an encounter. For example, one bandit gang might be an unruly mob of braggarts, while the members of another gang are always on edge and ready to flee at the first sign of danger.

entries.caption: Personnalité des monstres
rows: Boastful; makes a show of bravery but runs from danger
Disorderly; poorly trained and easily rattled

entries.name: Relations de monstres
entries: Encounters with groups of monsters can be more interesting if rivalries, hatreds, or attachments exist among the monsters in the group. The death of a much-revered leader might throw its followers into a frenzy. On the other hand, a monster might flee if its hunting companion is killed, or a mistreated toady might be eager to surrender and betray its boss in return for its life. You can use the Monster Relationships table to inspire such relationships within a monster group.

entries.caption: Relations de monstres
rows: Two monsters have a bitter rivalry; each wants the other to suffer.
One monster, bullied by the others, hangs back and flees at the first opportunity.
One monster is revered or even worshiped by the others, who will die for it.
One monster is admired by the group; its allies try to impress or help it.
One monster cares only for itself and not the rest of the group.
One monster bullies the others; it forces them into danger, but they want it defeated.

entries.name: Tactiques réactives
entries: A great way to make an adventure location feel alive—particularly an organized base or stronghold—is to allow its denizens to react to the presence of the adventurers. Once they are aware of trespassers, sapient creatures might either fortify their own locations or leave those locations to assist colleagues and expel the invaders.

Take a copy of the adventure map, and pencil in the locations of all its inhabitants to give yourself a sense of where they're located relative to each other. When the adventurers engage in combat or any other noisy activity, assume that nearby creatures hear the noise and are alerted to the adventurers' presence. (Creatures that can't hear might be alerted by vibrations or other sensory cues.) Once alerted, a creature has several options:

items.name: Embuscade
items.entry: La créature quitte sa position actuelle et prend position près de celle des aventuriers, espérant les surprendre à l'improviste. Les embusqués tentent de se cacher et, une fois cachés, profitent de tout moment opportun pour attaquer.

items.name: Se fortifier
items.entry: La créature tente de fortifier sa position en utilisant des meubles ou des objets lourds pour bloquer portes ou entrées. Augmentez le DD pour forcer une porte bloquée de 3, et les passages bloqués à la hâte constituent un {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|XPHB|terrain difficile}. Une créature dotée d'une attaque à distance qui choisit cette option cherche un couvert dans sa position.

items.name: Se cacher / Fuir
items.entry: Si possible, la créature se cache dans sa position actuelle, espérant éviter tout aventurier qui y entrerait. S'il n'y a nulle part où se cacher, la créature fuit vers un lieu plus éloigné des aventuriers ou vers un lieu voisin occupé par ses alliés. Si une créature en fuite atteint des alliés, ceux-ci sont immédiatement alertés de la présence des aventuriers ; déterminez la réaction de ces alliés.

items.name: Enquêter
items.entry: La créature accourt vers le bruit de la perturbation pour enquêter, rejoignant peut-être tout combat en cours. Une créature qui passe près d'un allié en se déplaçant pour enquêter sur une perturbation peut demander à cet allié de l'accompagner.

entries: If you can't decide what an alerted creature should do, have it make a {@dc 10} Wisdom saving throw. On a successful save, the creature either investigates or lays an ambush; on a failed save, it hides or fortifies its location. When dealing with a group of creatures, the leader makes this saving throw on behalf of the entire group.
As creatures employ reactive tactics, make notes about their new locations on your adventure map.

entries.name: Défenseurs préparés
entries: Sapient creatures that have reason to believe their lair is likely to be invaded might set up a defense. Reasons to set up a defense include the following:

items: Adventurers invaded the lair recently and retreated.
Scouts affiliated with the lair's denizens noticed the adventurers heading toward the lair.
A spy in a nearby settlement overheard or discovered the adventurers' plans and alerted the lair's occupants.

entries: Prepared defenders commonly use one or more of the following tactics:

items.name: Embuscades et barricades
items.entry: Certains défenseurs peuvent quitter leurs positions d'origine pour des positions où ils peuvent se cacher près de passages stratégiques. Les défenseurs peuvent aussi utiliser meubles et débris pour obturer les passages, espérant canaliser les envahisseurs vers des points forts préparés.

items.name: Sentinelles et alarmes
items.entry: Certaines créatures peuvent quitter leurs emplacements attitrés pour des emplacements leur permettant de surveiller les entrées du repaire. Si possible, ces créatures peuvent se munir d'une alarme telle qu'une corne ou un gong improvisé (une marmite vide, peut-être). À la première vue d'intrus, elles donnent l'alerte, avertissant les alliés proches afin que ces camarades puissent employer les tactiques réactives décrites ci-dessus.

items.name: Pièges
items.entry: Les défenseurs peuvent placer des pièges supplémentaires, comme des filets chuteurs, partout dans le repaire (voir « {@book Traps|XDMG|2|Pièges} » au {@book chapitre 3|XDMG|2}).

entries: If the denizens of an adventure location employ any of these tactics, update your map as appropriate.

entries.name: Rythme et tension des rencontres
entries: A good story hooks you in with an interesting introduction, builds tension steadily throughout the story, then reaches a climactic conclusion. It's not always easy to mimic that structure in an adventure where the players control their characters' actions, but you can use the encounters you plan to build tension toward a climax.

Each encounter in an adventure is an opportunity to make the characters' situation more complex and urgent, with more significant consequences. Successive encounters raise the tension in an adventure naturally, as characters spend their limited resources. Variety also contributes to a sense of escalating tension. Build variety into your encounters in three ways:

items.name: Varier le type de rencontre
items.entry: Utilisez un mélange de rencontres d'interaction sociale, d'exploration et de combat. Les différents types de rencontres procurent différentes quantités de tension (les rencontres de combat offrent généralement la plus forte), mais ils se ressentent aussi très différemment et peuvent avoir des enjeux radicalement différents.

items.name: Varier la difficulté des rencontres
items.entry: Incluez des rencontres de difficulté faible, modérée et élevée. Un mélange de rencontres de difficulté faible et modérée au début de l'aventure peut mener à un combat culminant de difficulté élevée, peut-être contre le vilain principal de l'aventure ou une autre menace.

items.name: Varier les menaces
items.entry: Construisez les rencontres avec différentes menaces. Si les personnages explorent un temple kuo-toa et s'attendent donc à ce que de nombreuses rencontres incluent divers kuo-toa, cherchez des occasions d'inclure différents monstres pouvant servir de gardes, d'animaux de compagnie ou d'alliés aux kuo-toa. Incluez une variété de dangers environnementaux, de périls et de pièges dans les rencontres d'exploration, et utilisez des PNJ aux personnalités et objectifs différents dans les rencontres d'interaction sociale.

entries.name: Urgence et repos
entries: While successive encounters increase tension, taking a Short Rest relaxes the tension somewhat, as characters have a chance to replenish some of their resources. In many adventures, though, the characters and their players have a sense that they need to act quickly to deal with the situation presented by the adventure. This creates tension between the need to rest and the sense that things are getting worse while the characters are resting.

You can influence the pace and tension of your adventure by determining where and when the characters can rest. If the characters are exploring a vast dungeon, consider scattering a few small rooms with only one door, where the characters can bar the door and reasonably expect to spend an hour or even a night resting in safety. On the flip side, cautious characters might try to take a Short Rest between every encounter, never really straining their resources. It's OK to interrupt those rests once in a while to maintain a sense of tension or to heighten the urgency, making it clear that even an hour spent resting could jeopardize their chances of success.

entries.name: Relâcher la pression
entries: It is possible to dial up the urgency to the point that the players feel they don't have time to investigate the interesting details they encounter in the world. When this happens, consider using a helpful NPC to take some of the pressure off. A wise elder might advise them that the situation is not as urgent as they fear, a whimsical Fey being might use magical mischief to force them to slow down, or a kindly Celestial could tell them they're taking the concerns of the mortal world just a bit too seriously.

entries.name: Rencontres aléatoires

entries.title: Des lumières mystérieuses scintillent dans un lac de montagne isolé, attirant les aventuriers vers l'exploration

entries: Random encounters are randomly determined encounters that don't occur in a fixed location. The options are often presented in a table. When a random encounter occurs, you roll a die and consult the table to determine what the party encounters. Sample random encounter tables appear in the adventure examples later in this chapter. Similar tables appear in many published adventures and rulebooks, and you can easily create your own by following these examples.
Handled well, random encounters can serve a variety of useful purposes.

entries.name: Créer un sentiment d'urgence
entries: Wandering monsters encourage characters to keep moving and to find a safe place to rest. (Sometimes you can create a sense of danger and urgency by rolling dice behind your DM screen, even without an actual encounter!)

entries.name: Épuiser les ressources des personnages
entries: By draining the party's Hit Points and spell slots, leaving the adventurers feeling underpowered and vulnerable, random encounters can build tension in an adventure.

entries.name: Établir l'atmosphère
entries: Thematic links among monsters appearing in random encounters create a tone and an atmosphere that define the environment the characters are exploring. For example, an encounter table filled with bats, wraiths, giant spiders, and zombies creates a sense of horror and suggests the possibility of even more terrifying foes.

entries.name: Fournir de l'aide
entries: Some random encounters can benefit the characters instead of hindering or harming them. Helpful creatures might give the characters useful information or assistance.

entries.name: Renforcer les thèmes de la campagne
entries: Random encounters can remind the players of the major themes and conflicts in your campaign. For example, if a war between two nations is a major conflict in your campaign, you might design random encounter tables to reinforce the ever-present threat of that conflict, including encounters with bedraggled troops returning from battle, refugees fleeing invaders, lone messengers riding for the front lines, enemy war parties, and so on.

entries.name: Une vie propre
entries: Sometimes a random encounter that starts off incidental can become important to the story. A random encounter with a wandering ogre might end with the ogre offering to help the characters get where they need to go, or the ogre might have something in a nearby den that is significant to the adventure story—a prisoner, a stolen item, or important information. Or the players might find the ogre's personality delightful, prompting you to make the ogre a more important part of the story.

entries.name: Conclure
entries: The climactic ending of an adventure fulfills the promise of all that came before. The best climax is one the players see coming, so if a dragon is the mastermind behind all the nefarious activity happening in an adventure, having the dragon's minions mention the nature of their boss sets up the coming climactic encounter.
Although the climax must hinge on the successes and failures of the characters up to that moment, the Adventure Climax table can provide suggestions to help you shape the end of your adventure.

entries.caption: Climax d'aventure
rows: The adventurers confront a villain and a group of minions in a battle to the finish.
The adventurers chase a villain while dodging obstacles designed to thwart them, leading to a final confrontation in the villain's refuge.
The actions of the adventurers or a villain result in a cataclysmic event that the adventurers must escape.
The adventurers race to the site where a villain is bringing a master plan to its conclusion, arriving just as that plan is about to be completed.
A villain and two or three lieutenants perform separate rites in a large room. The adventurers must disrupt all the rites.
An ally betrays the adventurers as they're about to achieve their goal. (Use this climax carefully, and don't overuse it.)
A portal opens to another plane of existence. Creatures on the other side spill out, forcing the adventurers to close the portal while dealing with a villain at the same time.
The dungeon begins to collapse while a villain attempts to escape in the chaos.
The adventurers must choose whether to pursue a fleeing villain or save an NPC they care about or a group of innocents.
Just when the characters think the main threat is defeated, it transforms into a different monster or a more powerful form.

entries.name: Dénouement
entries: In most stories, there's a period after the climax, in which loose plot threads are tied up and everything is explained. An adventure might also include this kind of denouement: time to discover what treasure is in the dragon's hoard, an award ceremony where the queen gives medals to the victorious heroes, or even a time to mourn adventuring companions who didn't survive the battle.

The denouement can also be an opportunity for the players to identify loose threads that haven't been tied up—threads that can lead them into the next adventure. The "{@book Episodes and Serials|XDMG|4|Episodes and Serials}" section in {@book chapter 5|XDMG|4} offers suggestions for weaving these connecting threads.

entries.name: Récompenses d'aventure
entries: For some characters, the prospect of material reward is their primary reason for going on adventures. For others it's a welcome added benefit to pursuing their other goals.
{@book Chapter 7|XDMG|6} describes different kinds of treasure, but see also "{@book Marks of Prestige|XDMG|2|Marks of Prestige}" in {@book chapter 3|XDMG|2} for other rewards you might use.
The following sections describe how treasure is typically dispersed in an adventure.

entries.name: Trésor individuel
entries: Characters might find small amounts of treasure in the pockets, pouches, or personal stashes of individual monsters. Even if a monster doesn't intentionally collect treasure, characters might find scattered coins and other monetary treasure left behind by the monster's previous victims.

You can use the Random Individual Treasure table to determine how much treasure a single monster has based on its Challenge Rating (CR). The table includes the average total in parentheses, which you can use instead of rolling. To determine the total amount of treasure for a group of similar creatures, you can roll once and multiply the total by the number of creatures in the group.

entries.name: Caches de trésor
entries: Adventurers sometimes discover large caches of treasure, the accumulated wealth of a large group of creatures or the belongings of a single powerful creature that hoards valuables. The Random Treasure Hoard table can help you create such a cache. When determining the contents of a hoard belonging to one monster, use the row for that monster's Challenge Rating (CR). When the hoard belongs to a large group of monsters, use the CR of the monster that leads the group. Each row includes average results for monetary treasure, which you can use instead of rolling. To create a hoard for a monster that is particularly fond of amassing treasure (such as a dragon), you can roll twice on the table or roll once and double the total.

As a rough benchmark, aim to roll on the Random Treasure Hoard table about once per game session. Use the guidelines in {@book chapter 7|XDMG|6} to determine which magic items are in the hoard (see "{@book Awarding Magic Items|XDMG|6|Awarding Magic Items}" and "{@book Random Magic Items|XDMG|6|Random Magic Item Rarity}").

entries.title: Une bataille culminant au Temple du Mal élémentaire clôt une aventure de façon spectaculaire

entries.name: Récompenses de quête
entries: Sometimes, characters are paid for completing a quest. To determine a suitable quest reward, roll once on the Random Treasure Hoard table, using the characters' level for the Challenge Rating (CR).

entries.name: Préférences de trésor des monstres
entries: The {@book Monster Manual|XMM} gives treasure preferences for monsters in that book. These preferences are categorized as follows:

items.name: Tout
items.entry: Le monstre possède une cache de trésor dont vous déterminez le contenu en lançant sur la table de la Cache de trésor aléatoire. Le trésor monétaire peut prendre la forme de {@book pièces|XDMG|6|monnaies}, de {@book lingots|XDMG|6|lingots de commerce}, de {@book marchandises|XDMG|6|marchandises}, de {@book gemmes|XDMG|6|pierres précieuses} ou d'{@book objets d'art|XDMG|6|objets d'art} (tous décrits au {@book chapitre 7|XDMG|6}). Les objets magiques peuvent appartenir à n'importe quel thème ou catégorie de trésor (voir « {@book Treasure Themes|XDMG|6|Thèmes de trésor} » et « {@book Magic Item Categories|XDMG|6|Catégories d'objets magiques} » au {@book chapitre 7|XDMG|6}).

items.name: Individuel
items.entry: Le monstre ne possède pas de cache de trésor ; il peut toutefois avoir un trésor monétaire, que vous déterminez en lançant sur la table du {@book Random Individual Treasure|XDMG|3|Trésor individuel aléatoire}. Ce trésor peut prendre la forme de pièces, de lingots de commerce, de marchandises, de gemmes ou d'objets d'art (tous décrits au {@book chapitre 7|XDMG|6}).

items.name: Thème de trésor (Arcanes, Armements, Instruments ou Reliques)
items.entry: Le monstre possède une cache de trésor orientée vers un thème particulier (voir « {@book Treasure Themes|XDMG|6|Thèmes de trésor} » au {@book chapitre 7|XDMG|6}). Vous pouvez déterminer la taille de la cache en lançant sur la table de la {@book Random Treasure Hoard|XDMG|3|Cache de trésor aléatoire}. Si la cache contient des objets magiques, utilisez les {@book indications et tables|XDMG|6|Rareté des objets magiques aléatoires} du {@book chapitre 7|XDMG|6} pour déterminer chacun d'eux.

entries.name: Exemples d'aventures
entries: This section contains example adventures that demonstrate the principles described throughout the chapter. Each provides enough information for you to run a one-session adventure, with the help of the maps in {@book Appendix B|XDMG|9} and the monster stat blocks in the {@book Monster Manual|XMM}.
Each adventure in this section includes the following information:

items.name: Titre
items.entry: Un titre d'aventure peut vous aider à organiser vos notes de campagne, et si vous le partagez avec vos joueurs, il peut donner le ton de ce qui les attend.

items.name: Niveau des personnages
items.entry: Chaque aventure précise le niveau des personnages visés. La difficulté des rencontres de chaque aventure est calibrée pour quatre personnages de ce niveau. Vous pouvez utiliser ces aventures pour des personnages de niveau supérieur ou inférieur, ou pour des groupes plus grands ou plus petits. Les rencontres risquent toutefois d'être plus faciles ou plus difficiles que prévu si vous ne les ajustez pas.

items.name: Situation
items.entry: Chaque aventure expose ce qui se passe — la situation que les aventuriers sont appelés à gérer. Voir « {@book Lay Out the Premise|XDMG|3|Établir le postulat} » plus tôt dans ce chapitre.

items.name: Amorce
items.entry: Chaque aventure propose une façon d'attirer les personnages dans l'aventure. Voir « {@book Draw In the Players|XDMG|3|Impliquer les joueurs} » plus tôt dans ce chapitre.

items.name: Rencontres
items.entry: Le reste de la description de chaque aventure est une série de rencontres. Le texte décrit le lieu où la rencontre se produit, renvoyant souvent aux cartes de l'{@book annexe B|XDMG|9}, ainsi que tout événement déclencheur susceptible de provoquer la rencontre. Les noms de monstres en {@b gras} renvoient aux blocs de statistiques du {@book Monster Manual|XMM}. Certaines rencontres précisent aussi le trésor que les personnages peuvent trouver.

entries: Use your imagination to bring the locations and encounters to life, and build on the ideas the players bring to each encounter. Alter these outlines freely to suit your tastes—and those of your players—and your ideas for your campaign.

entries.name: Une campagne pour débuter
entries: You can use the adventures in this section to get a new campaign off the ground. These adventures are linked to locations near the {@book Free City of Greyhawk|XDMG|4|Free City of Greyhawk}, as described in {@book chapter 5|XDMG|4}. You can run the first three adventures in sequence, having the characters gain a level after each adventure. They might return to their home base in the city between adventures, or they could travel to Greyhawk after they complete "{@book The Winged God|XDMG|3|The Winged God}." Use the encounters and interactions the characters have in these early levels, and the situations that interest your players, to plan later adventures.

entries.name: Le ruisseau souillé
entries: {@i Adventure for Level 1 Characters}

items.name: Situation
items.entry: Un champignon alien dans une grotte pollue le ruisseau qui coule devant le village de Haut-Ery. Le champignon a engendré des créatures viles dans la grotte et aux alentours.

items.name: Amorce
items.entry: Les habitants de Haut-Ery remarquent des pousses fongiques sur les berges et une couche de crasse sur l'eau. Les personnages peuvent habiter le village, ou un contact de la Cité libre de Grabenhorn peut leur demander d'enquêter.

entries.name: Rencontres
entries: The adventure consists of these encounters.

entries.name: La première confluence
entries: A mile upstream from the village, a stream flows into the river from a little wood on the river's south side. Characters can tell that this stream is the source of the pollution.

entries.name: Remonter le courant
entries: Borogrove, a kindly {@creature Treant|XMM}, keeps watch over the wood and meets the characters as they follow the polluted stream. He knows the source of the corruption is inside a cave that the stream spills out of. He gives the characters a magic acorn. If swallowed, the acorn conveys the benefits of a {@item Potion de soins|XDMG} and the {@spell Restauration partielle|XPHB} spell.

entries.name: Buissons raméens
entries: Just outside the cave, the characters encounter six {@creature Fléau des brindilles|XMM|Twig Blights}.

entries.name: La grotte corrompue
entries: Use the Underdark Warren map in {@book Appendix B|XDMG|9|Underdark Warren} for the corrupted cave. Ignore the secret door and the inner chambers behind it. Close off the tunnels leading off the map to the south, east, and north. The characters enter the cave in the southeast, following the stream. The cave's main features and inhabitants are as follows:

items.name: Entrance
items.entry: Un {@creature Shrieker Fungus|XMM} juste à l'intérieur de l'entrée de la grotte alerte les habitants de l'arrivée des personnages. En faction près de l'entrée et prompts à répondre au cri du champignon glapissant se trouvent quatre {@creature Bullywug Warrior|XMM|guerriers bullywugs} couverts de pousses fongiques.

items.name: L'ours en furie
items.entry: Dans une grotte latérale au sud-est se trouve un {@creature Ours brun|XMM} qui a bu au ruisseau. Il est en colère car l'eau l'a rendu malade. Si les personnages parviennent à lui faire manger le gland de Borogrove ou autrement à le débarrasser de la condition {@condition Empoisonné|XPHB}, l'ours récupère immédiatement et les laisse tranquilles.

items.name: Le repaire de l'ooze
items.entry: À l'extrémité nord du ruisseau se trouvent un {@creature Gluant gris|XMM|ooze gris psychique} et six {@creature Stirge|XMM|stirges}. Après avoir vaincu ces créatures, les personnages peuvent détruire le champignon en forme de cerveau dans l'eau, qui est la source de la corruption. S'ils le font, chaque personnage gagne un bonus de 100 PX.

entries.name: Le retour
entries: As they leave the wood, the characters encounter Borogrove again. If they used his acorn, he gives them another one. If they purified the source of the stream, he gives them a {@item Bâton aux fleurs|XDMG} in gratitude.

entries.name: Soucis de mineurs
entries: {@i Adventure for Level 2 Characters}

items.name: Situation
items.entry: Après que des mineurs ont percé un tunnel de l'Outreterre, un {@creature Horreur à crochet|XMM} s'est introduit dans la mine et s'y est retrouvé piégé. Il a dévoré quelques mineurs, et les autres sont trop terrifiés par les claquements résonnant dans la mine pour traquer le prédateur.

items.name: Amorce
items.entry: La maire du village de Pierre-Noire, Kristryd Splitanvil (un nain {@creature Tough|XMM} Loyal Bon), engage les aventuriers — peut-être en raison de la manière adroite dont ils ont géré la situation dans « {@book The Fouled Stream|XDMG|3|Le ruisseau souillé} » — pour s'occuper du monstre dans les mines. Elle offre une précieuse {@item Topaze|XDMG} d'une valeur de 500 po aux aventuriers qui tueront la créature ou la chasseront.

entries.name: Rencontres
entries: The adventure consists of these encounters.

entries.name: Explorer la mine
entries: Use the Mine map in {@book Appendix B|XDMG|9|Mine}. In the weeks since the miners abandoned the place, pests have flourished in the tunnels. Each time the characters enter a distinct area of the mine, roll on the following table.

rows: Four {@creature Fungus violet|XMM|Violet Fungi} and one {@creature Rôdeur des rouilles|XMM}
One {@creature Araignée géante|XMM} and two {@creature Nuée d'insectes|XMM|Swarms of Insects} (spiders)
A patch of {@hazard Moisi jaune|XDMG} (see "{@book Hazards|XDMG|2|Hazards}" in {@book chapter 3|XDMG|2}) on a miner's remains

entries.name: Sons de la terreur
entries: The first time this encounter occurs, the characters hear eerie clacking and scraping noises echoing in the mine shafts and notice gouges in the walls. The second time, they find the source of those sounds and markings—the {@creature Horreur à crochet|XMM}. The creature is hungry, but what it really wants is to find its way back to the Underdark. It retreats from a fight that is going badly for it.

entries.name: Liaison avec l'Outreterre
entries: The tunnel in the southeast corner of the bottom level of the mine is where the miners accidentally connected to an Underdark tunnel. The hook horror entered the mine through a hole in the wall, but the hole closed behind it in a cascade of rubble. If the characters clear away the rubble from the hole, they hear clacking and scraping from the other side. The hook horror hears it too and hurries here to rejoin its kin. As long as the characters stay out of its way, it ignores them as it scrambles back through the hole, never to plague the mine again. Each character then earns a bonus 200 XP.

entries.name: Le dieu ailé
entries: {@i Adventure for Level 3 Characters}

items.name: Situation
items.entry: Il y a quelques semaines, un {@creature Dragonnet rouge|XMM} a chassé une bande de kobolds de leur network pour s'approprier les lieux comme repaire. Maintenant, certains kobolds sèment le trouble dans les collines des Cairn. Ils pillent les marchands, espérant que le dragon les laissera rentrer chez eux en guise de serviteurs loyaux.

items.name: Amorce
items.entry: Un marchand nommé Nondy Barducks (un gnome {@creature Roturier|XMM} Loyal Neutre) engage les personnages pour escorter son charrette jusqu'au village minier reculé de Lac-de-Diamant, qui se trouve justement à proximité du nouveau repaire du dragon. Nondy a été détroussé par des kobolds lors de son dernier voyage et il veut une protection cette fois. Il propose de payer chaque personnage 150 po.

entries.name: Rencontres
entries: The adventure consists of these encounters.

entries.name: Bandits kobolds
entries: Along the road, the wagon is surrounded by eight {@creature Kobold Warrior|XMM|Kobold Warriors} (Neutral) who demand that the merchant surrender his goods. In combat, the kobolds shout things like "For the Winged God!" and "Fight to reclaim our home!" If four of them fall in battle, the remaining kobolds try to flee. Any captured kobold explains the situation.

entries.name: Kobolds suppliants
entries: If the characters continue on their way without pursuing the kobolds, twelve {@creature Kobold Warrior|XMM|Kobold Warriors} (including any survivors of the first encounter) and six {@creature Kobold ailé|XMM|Winged Kobolds} (all Neutral) approach the wagon. These kobolds humbly ask the adventurers to help them. They promise to return the goods they stole from Nondy if the adventurers drive off the dragon.

entries.name: Camp kobold
entries: If the adventurers follow fleeing kobolds, they can find the kobolds' camp on a nearby outcropping. The kobolds there don't fight, though, instead begging the adventurers to help them (as in "Kobold Supplicants" above).

entries.name: Le repaire du dragon
entries: Use the Volcanic Caves map in {@book Appendix B|XDMG|9|Volcanic Caves} for the dragon's lair, but close off passages to keep the lair small. Near the entrance, the characters encounter a gang of four {@creature Méphrite de magma|XMM|Magma Mephits} and three {@creature Méphrite de fumée|XMM|Smoke Mephits}, drawn to the lair by the magic of the dragon.
In the inner cave, the troublesome {@creature Dragonnet rouge|XMM} rests on its little hoard:

items: Crate holding Nondy's stolen goods (worth 400 GP)
Two {@item Spell Scroll|XDMG|Spell Scrolls} ({@spell Alarme|XPHB} and {@spell Compréhension des langues|XPHB})

entries: If the characters defeat or drive off the dragon, each of them earns a bonus 400 XP.

entries.name: Les cornes de la Bête
entries: {@i Adventure for Level 5 Characters}

items.name: Situation
items.entry: Une ruine depuis longtemps oubliée passerait pour renfermer un Artefact infernal appelé les Cornes de la Bête. Un vilain espère s'emparer de l'Artefact et en faire un terrible usage.

items.name: Amorce
items.entry: Un modeste marchand humain nommé Melchis (en secret un {@creature Fiend Cultist|XMM} Chaotique Mauvais dévoué à {@book Iuz|XDMG|8|Iuz}) engage les personnages pour l'escorter lors d'une expédition visant à trouver un temple antique perdu dans la jungle. Il propose de les payer un total de 2 000 po en lingots de commerce — la moitié à l'arrivée au temple, l'autre moitié à leur retour sain et sauf en civilisation — et promet de les appuyer avec ce qu'il prétend être une « capacité magique limitée ».

entries.name: Rencontres
entries: You can use the poster map of the world of Greyhawk for this adventure; the temple is located near the southern edge of the map, in the Amedio Jungle. The journey unfolds in three stages (see "{@book Travel|XDMG|1|Travel}" in {@book chapter 2|XDMG|1}), culminating in the discovery of the ruins and the artifact.

entries.name: Étape 1
entries: Melchis hires a ship to carry the party to the Amedio Jungle. Use the map to determine how long the sea voyage takes, depending on where the adventurers begin the trip and figuring that the ship covers about 1½ hexes per day. Near the end of the trip, as the ship crosses Jeklea Bay, it's attacked by a group of {@variantrule Hostile [Attitude]|XPHB|Hostile} sahuagin, including two {@creature Sahuagin Priest|XMM|Sahuagin Priests}, six {@creature Sahuagin Warrior|XMM|Sahuagin Warriors}, and a {@creature Élémentaire de l'Eau|XMM}. (Assume the ship's crew stays out of the way of these terrifying monsters and lets the characters and Melchis deal with this threat.) Stage 1 ends when Melchis and the characters row a launch ashore.

entries.name: Étape 2
entries: Melchis leads the characters into the jungle, aiming for the shore of the lake. This stage covers about 180 miles through the dense forest. Each day of the journey, roll once on the following table to determine what the characters encounter on their journey, if anything.

rows: An {@variantrule Indifferent [Attitude]|XPHB|Indifferent} {@creature Singe géant|XMM} protects its territory; its primary concern is getting the party to leave.
A {@variantrule Hostile [Attitude]|XPHB|Hostile} {@creature T-Rex|XMM} is on the hunt and tries to eat the characters.
Three {@creature Allosaure|XMM|Allosauruses} are hunting in the jungle; they are {@variantrule Hostile [Attitude]|XPHB|Hostile} and treat the party as prey.

Two {@creature Ankylosaure|XMM|Ankylosauruses} tromp through the forest nearby. They are territorial and aggressive but {@variantrule Indifferent [Attitude]|XPHB|Indifferent}, and they won't pursue a fleeing party.

A band of humans, including a {@creature Warrior Veteran|XMM} and eight {@creature Warrior Infantry|XMM}, watch the party. They are {@variantrule Indifferent [Attitude]|XPHB|Indifferent}; they live in the jungle and aren't used to seeing other people.
Four {@creature Minotaur of Baphomet|XMM|Minotaurs of Baphomet} prowl the jungle looking for Humanoids they can capture and bring back to the temple.

entries.name: Étape 3
entries: Once the characters reach the edge of the lake, Melchis leads them southwest along the shore until they find the ruin. This stage covers 90 miles through coastal terrain. The second day of the journey, {@hazard Fortes précipitations|XDMG|heavy rain} obscures vision and creates {@hazard Fosse de sable mouvant|XDMG|quicksand pits} (see "{@book Environmental Effects|XDMG|2|Environmental Effects}" and "{@book Hazards|XDMG|2|Hazards}" in {@book chapter 3|XDMG|2}). The front rank of the party might fall into a quicksand pit while two {@creature Crocodile géant|XMM|Giant Crocodiles} attack at the same time. The rest of the journey passes without incident.

entries.name: Les ruines
entries: For the ruins, use the western half of the ground floor of the Dungeon Hideout map in {@book Appendix B|XDMG|9|Dungeon Hideout}, and ignore the stairs leading to the lower levels. Dwelling in the ruins are six {@creature Minotaur of Baphomet|XMM|Minotaurs of Baphomet} who are Hostile to all intruders. They are spread out around the ruins but come quickly when they hear combat.

entries.name: L'Artefact
entries: The Horns of the Beast—a jagged crown made from the horns of demons and wild animals—rests on a pedestal in the northwest corner of the ruins. Melchis immediately attempts to seize the Artifact and place it on his head. If he does, he is transformed into a {@creature Hezrou|XMM} and tries to kill the characters. A character who dons the Artifact is cursed with {@book Demonic Possession|XDMG|2|Demonic Possession} (see "{@book Curses and Magical Contagions|XDMG|2|Curses and Magical Contagions}" in {@book chapter 3|XDMG|2}). The Artifact can't be removed from the character's head until a {@spell Délivrance de la malédiction|XPHB} spell is cast on the character. If the characters defeat Melchis and search him, they find a {@item Sac contenant|XDMG} containing twelve 5-pound gold trade bars (worth 250 GP each) and a {@item Spell Scroll|XDMG} of {@spell Cercle de téléportation|XPHB}. The scroll also contains the sigil sequence for a permanent teleportation circle. At the end of the adventure, each character earns a bonus 1,000 XP.

entries.name: Détruire l'Artefact
entries: The Horns of the Beast can be destroyed only by dropping it in the {@book River Oceanus|XDMG|5|River Oceanus}, which flows through the Upper Planes (see {@book chapter 6|XDMG|5}). A character can learn this by casting {@spell Identification|XPHB} on the Artifact.

entries.name: Le bal boréal
entries: {@i Adventure for Level 7 Characters}

entries.title: Minsc, Boo et Delina naviguent les intrigues du bal boréal

items.name: Situation
